# Veritas: neatHack build log

## Project

Veritas is an autonomous dependency intelligence and remediation agent for JavaScript/TypeScript repositories. It finds dependency changes that matter, proves whether they affect a given repo, writes a fix in an isolated workspace, recovers from failed attempts, and verifies the result.

Tagline: Verified changes. Reliable software.

Full plan: [VERITAS_PLAN.md](VERITAS_PLAN.md)

## Team

Solo.

## Stack

- TypeScript on Node.js
- Models through the hackathon LiteLLM endpoint (OpenAI-compatible)
- neatlogs for tracing agent runs
- Entire for checkpoints and entire-graph
- cfo.ai for the business plan
- SQLite for agent state

## Build log

### 2026-10-10

Completed:
- Read the hackathon rules and the docs for neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai. Wrote VERITAS_PLAN.md.
- Installed Entire CLI 0.11.4 from the official GitHub release (checksum verified) and the entire-graph plugin v0.4.0.
- Measured on the same case, same model (`claude-haiku`), before (`evidence/bench/dev-m5.json`) and after (`evidence/bench/after-neatlogs-fix-express.json`):

  | express 4 to 5 repair | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | `apply_edit` calls | 14 | 3 |
  | Refused edits | 12 | 0 |
  | Cost | $0.1401 | $0.0533 |
  | Duration | 59 s | 38 s |
  | Result | fixed, acceptance passes | fixed, acceptance passes |

  One case, one run each side; the full benchmark comparison is still to come.
- Limits met in neatlogs: the neat AI chat ran out of length twice while trying to rewrite larger files for a pull request, and succeeded when the change was limited to one 48-line file. neatlogs shows $0 cost on the agent's traces although tokens are correct. The project still reports tier `free` and an empty repository field through the MCP server, although GitHub and Claude Code are connected in the UI.
- Tests that ran: `npx vitest run` — 69 passed. `npx tsc --noEmit` clean.
- Entire check at the end of the day: 32 of 37 commits carry a checkpoint and all are pushed (the others are the first two commits and GitHub's merge commits). The repository is now mirrored in Entire on two clusters with public visibility, after the Entire account was linked to GitHub; `entire search` returns results from the repository's history and `entire recap` shows 32 sessions and 32 checkpoints. Outputs in `evidence/entire/`.
- Checked in a logged-out browser: the project and its checkpoints are publicly viewable at https://entire.io/gh/Milliebanned/Veritas, so judges can open them directly.
- Added `README.md`: what Veritas does, how each state works, how the three tools are used, results so far, how to run it, and what is not built yet.
- Entire's graph in the build itself is still weak: `entire graph stats` reports 15 graph calls against 178 search-and-read calls, a graph-first rate of 0%, and only 3 of those graph calls came after the earlier promise to use it first. This has to change in the next milestone and will be measured again.

### 2026-10-11

Completed:
- Verification rules (rest of Milestone 6). A repair is `verified` only when: the tests passed before the upgrade; the failure was reproduced when code had to change; the tests pass now; no fewer tests pass than before; and `entire graph verify` judges the run as passing when it is available. Files changed outside those impact analysis flagged, and runs where per-test comparison was not possible, are recorded as caveats. A fix that passes its tests but breaks a rule is reported as `unresolved`.
- The report. REPORT is now a real state: it assembles findings, sources (read from the source versus inferred), affected sites, each repair's test runs, every attempt with its plan, diff and diagnosis, the verification checks, what could not be checked, remaining risk and cost. No model is involved. `veritas report <id>` prints it.
- Benchmark case 9, built to be harder (`bench/cases/09-node-fetch-timeout`): node-fetch 2 to 3 in a project that relies on the removed `timeout` option and on the error type a timeout used to raise. Three changes are needed and each failure only shows once the one before is fixed. Confirmed with `node bench/reproduce.mjs`: baseline passes, the upgrade fails, the reference fix passes the tests and the acceptance test.
- Tests that ran: `npx vitest run` — 78 passed, 0 failed. `npx tsc --noEmit` clean.

A real failure (evidence item: "a run where an action failed, showing the agent's next step"):
- First run of the agent on case 9, `claude-haiku` (`evidence/bench/m6-case09.json`, report in `evidence/reports/09-node-fetch-timeout-unresolved.md`, neatlogs trace `af018a75f8994e89807d0faf9f373dcf`): impact verdict correct, failure reproduced, then three repair attempts all failed and the finding was reported `unresolved`. 65 model calls, $0.41, 144 seconds.
- What the agent did after each failure: attempt 1 fixed the import; the diagnosis said the timeout error type had changed; attempt 2 changed the error check to `err.name === 'AbortError'`; the next diagnosis guessed `err.code === 'ABORT_ERR'`; attempt 3 tried that; the last diagnosis reversed it again. It stopped at the limit and said so. It did not claim a fix.
- Why it failed, from the record: none of the stored sources says the `timeout` option was removed. The v3.0.0 release note is two lines and points to a changelog; the upgrade guide that states the removal (`docs/v3-UPGRADE-GUIDE.md`) was never fetched, because the release links to it with the word "changelog", and only links mentioning migration or upgrade are followed. Without that fact every attempt left `timeout: timeoutMs` in place, so the request never timed out and the diagnoses went looking in the wrong file. The diagnosis role also cannot run anything, so its claims about the error object were guesses.
- Also seen: impact analysis flagged `test/status.test.js` as affected, which is a false positive on files (2 of 3 correct).
- Not fixed yet. This is the next problem to put through neatlogs.

Entire check (end of this milestone): the code graph was used first to locate the verify handler, the report stub and the patch result before any file was read. `entire graph stats` is recorded below this entry.
- Milestone 8, first part: the web app. A Fastify server (`npm run serve`) with a plain HTML and JavaScript interface, no build step. Screens: the list of investigations with a form to start one, and for each investigation the live state timeline with findings and sources, patch review (test runs before and after, verification checks, each attempt with its diff, Approve and Reject), the report, and the step history with retries and cost. Investigations run one at a time in the background. An optional shared access token protects the API.
- Approval is the only point at which anything leaves the workspace: for a GitHub repository each verified fix's branch is pushed and a pull request is opened, with the proof in its description; for a local repository the decision is recorded and the branch stays in the workspace. Pull request opening is written but has not been exercised against GitHub yet.
- Tested by running a real investigation through the web app's API (express case): verified fix, then approved. Screenshots of the five screens in `evidence/ui/`, taken with a headless browser.
- A bug found by that run, in the verification rule added earlier today: it rejected a good fix because `entire graph verify` answered "NO EFFECT — the target tests behave exactly as before your edit", and the code accepted only the word PASS. The unit tests had not caught it because their stand-in for the judge never returned that verdict. Fixed: only an explicit FAIL verdict blocks verification; a test covers NO EFFECT.
- A limit of `entire graph verify` with Node's built-in test runner, found while checking that bug: it reads the output as Jest-style, and it answered NO EFFECT even for a run where two tests newly failed, both with and without test timings in the output. So for these projects its verdict cannot be relied on to catch a regression; the project's own test run remains the source of truth, as planned. Not yet reported to Entire.
- Tests that ran: `npx vitest run` — 79 passed. `npx tsc --noEmit` clean.
- Second improvement through neatlogs: the case 9 failure. neatlogs had flagged the run ("Execution Failed") on its own. neat AI was given the trace and the cause found in the record (no stored source mentioned the removed `timeout` option) and opened pull request #5 as `neatlogs[bot]`, adding `src/tools/upgradeGuides.ts`: it lists a package repository's files and fetches Markdown upgrade and migration guides. Follow-up commits on the same pull request wire it into the release-notes step, keep only guides for the major versions being crossed, and add tests.
- The first rerun with that change did not succeed, and showed two further faults in the agent loop, both visible in the saved trace (`18937ea29f0a3f3ac0e3f48e0814a0af`): with the upgrade guide now in hand the repair agent knew what to do, but spent all 19 of its tool calls reading and searching, was then left with only the submit tool, submitted twice with nothing edited, and the investigation crashed. Fixed in the same pull request: the agent is told its tool budget and how many calls are left; the last 8 calls of a repair are reserved for editing; and an attempt that produces no edit is recorded as a failed attempt, which goes to diagnosis like any other, instead of ending the investigation.
- Measured on case 9, same model (`claude-haiku`), one run each (`evidence/bench/m6-case09.json` before, `evidence/bench/after-neatlogs-fix-case09.json` after; reports in `evidence/reports/`):

  | node-fetch 2 to 3, removed `timeout` option | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | Outcome | unresolved after 3 attempts | verified on attempt 1 |
  | Held-out acceptance test | fail | pass |
  | Sources stored for the finding | 2 | 3, including the upgrade guide |
  | Model calls | 65 | 22 |
  | Cost | $0.41 | $0.18 |
  | Duration | 144 s | 61 s |

- Still true: no repair has yet failed its tests and then recovered. Case 9 went from never fixed to fixed first time.
- Tests that ran: `npx vitest run` — 84 passed. `npx tsc --noEmit` clean.
- Server (Milestones 7 and 10). One EC2 `t3.large` in `us-east-1`, in a public subnet of `Hackathon_VPC`, 30 GB disk, Ubuntu 26.04. The first instance was launched in a private subnet and could not be reached; it was terminated and replaced. Installed: Docker 29.1.3, Node v24.21.0, Entire CLI 0.11.4 (checksum verified) with entire-graph v0.4.0. The repository's 84 tests pass on the server.
- The container sandbox ran for the first time. One fix was needed before it could: containers now run as the workspace's owner instead of root, so files they write can be cleaned up and committed.
- Full benchmark on the server, all nine cases, `claude-haiku`, project commands in Docker with no network for tests (`evidence/bench/server-v1-haiku.json`):

  | Metric | Result |
  |---|---|
  | Verdicts correct | 9 of 9 |
  | Fixable cases repaired, held-out acceptance test passing | 7 of 7, all on the first attempt |
  | Controls correct (false positives) | 2 of 2 (0) |
  | Findings backed by a source read from its URL | 11 of 11 |
  | Affected files, recall | 13 of 13 |
  | Affected files, precision | 13 of 17 |
  | Sandbox runs completed | 20 of 20 |
  | Crashes, repeated steps | 0, 0 |
  | Duration | 236 s |
  | Cost | $0.80 (107 model calls, 664,587 tokens) |

- For comparison, the first full run on October 10 (`evidence/bench/dev-m5.json`: eight cases, local sandbox, before the changes that came out of neatlogs) had 7 of 8 verdicts and 5 of 6 repairs, and case 9 on its first run was unresolved. The two runs differ in machine and sandbox as well as in the agent, so this is not a controlled comparison; the controlled before/after figures are the two single-case tables above.
- Worse than before: affected-file precision. Impact analysis now also flags files that do not need to change: test files in three cases, and in one case a file that only calls the affected one. Recall is complete. Not fixed.
- Cost per investigation is higher than on October 10 (about $0.09 to $0.16 for a breaking case, from about $0.05 to $0.14), partly from the longer upgrade-guide sources.
- The web app is running on the server at http://3.88.235.251:3210, behind a shared access token.
- Still not seen: a repair that fails its tests and then recovers. Every repair in this run succeeded on its first attempt.
- Entire check: `entire graph stats` now reports 22 graph calls (9 credited lookups) against 231 other search-and-read calls; the graph was used first for each code lookup in this milestone.
- Web app redesigned after the first version was judged too basic. It now has a public landing page (what Veritas does, the four questions, benchmark numbers read from the committed result file, how each tool is used), a card view of investigations, and an investigation page with a headline verdict, key numbers, the stages grouped into four phases, and restyled findings, patch review, report and history. Screenshots replaced in `evidence/ui/`.
- Sign in with GitHub, replacing the shared access token as the way in. With a GitHub OAuth app configured (`GITHUB_CLIENT_ID`, `GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET`), people sign in, pick one of their own public JavaScript or TypeScript repositories, see only their own investigations, and on approval the pull request is opened with their own GitHub access on their own repository. Each person is limited to 5 investigations a day and the whole service to 60, to protect the model budget. Sessions are kept server-side; the browser holds only an HttpOnly cookie. Written and type-checked; not yet exercised end to end, because the OAuth app does not exist yet. Without one, the server falls back to the access token.
- Tests that ran: `npx vitest run` — 84 passed. `npx tsc --noEmit` clean.
- Second redesign, after the dark version was judged generic. The site is now light and built around an original illustrated landscape generated in code (`web/scene.js`): mountains, a lake, forested shores, drifting clouds, birds and frosted glass tiles, with depth that follows the pointer and the scroll. A floating pill menu, one large headline, and the same sections below. The app's first screen was reorganised into one clear action (start an investigation: choose a repository or paste an address) with a three-step explanation and a plain list of investigations. No stock or third-party artwork is used.

Open problem (neatlogs platform, 2026-10-10):
- Traces sent after 12:53 UTC are accepted by neatlogs but never finish processing: the MCP server reports `status: processing`, `finalization_status: pending`, `span_count: 0` for all of them, including a two-span test trace. Only the first two traces of the day are readable.
- neatlogs' own SDK Doctor fails the same way: `neatlogs doctor --probe` passes every local check and then fails with `TRACE_READBACK_TIMEOUT`. Output saved in `evidence/neatlogs/doctor-probe-2026-10-10.json`. The SDK reports successful delivery with 0 dropped spans and 0 failed exports.
- Until it clears: every span is also written locally to `.veritas/spans/`, and Detections cannot be set up yet because neatlogs requires previewing them against finalized traces.
- `entire recap` and `entire activity` show no activity for the account although 17 checkpoints exist in the repository and on GitHub; `entire dispatch` and `entire review` need a coding-agent CLI on the PATH, which this machine's shell does not have.

Found in Milestone 3:
- The express 5.0.0 release notes do not list the removed methods; they link to a migration guide. INTEL now follows such links, so the removed APIs (`app.del`, `req.param`, `res.json(obj, status)`) are in the recorded source.
- A GitHub advisory can list several version ranges for one package, each with its own fix. The first version of the parser took the first range and reported the wrong fixed version for uuid 3.4.0 (12.0.1, correct is 11.1.1). It now uses the range that contains the installed version, with a test.
- uuid has no GitHub release for 7.0.0 and 8.0.0; those notes come from its `CHANGELOG.md`.
- One lodash advisory in the database was withdrawn in 2021 and is ignored.

Changed from the plan:
- State store uses Node's built-in `node:sqlite` instead of `better-sqlite3`. It avoids a native build on the dev machine and on EC2.
- The fallback impact provider is a source text scan, not the TypeScript compiler API.
- The inventory is read from the lockfile directly; `npm outdated` and `npm ls` are not used, so nothing has to be installed to list dependencies.

## Demo

Not built yet.

## Known limitations and next steps

- Every state is real, and there is a web interface. Case 9 is unresolved by the agent. No repair has yet failed and then recovered. Opening a pull request on approval has not been run against GitHub. Scored runs have not happened on the server.
- Impact accuracy is perfect on this benchmark, so it shows no room to improve yet. The repair stages are where failures are expected.
- Only direct dependencies are checked for breaking changes; advisories cover the whole installed tree.

A floating pill menu, one large headline, and the same sections below. The app's first screen was reorganised into one clear action (start an investigation: choose a repository or paste an address) with a three-step explanation and a plain list of investigations. No stock or third-party artwork is used.

- Traces sent after 12:53 UTC are accepted by neatlogs but never finish processing: the MCP server reports `status: processing`, `finalization_status: pending`, `span_count: 0` for all of them, including a two-span test trace. Only the first two traces of the day are readable.

Found in Milestone 3:

Changed from the plan:
- State store uses Node's built-in `node:sqlite` instead of `better-sqlite3`. It avoids a native build on the dev machine and on EC2.
- The fallback impact provider is a source text scan, not the TypeScript compiler API.
- The inventory is read from the lockfile directly; `npm outdated` and `npm ls` are not used, so nothing has to be installed to list dependencies.

Not built yet.

- Every state is real, and there is a web interface. Case 9 is unresolved by the agent. No repair has yet failed and then recovered. Opening a pull request on approval has not been run against GitHub. Scored runs have not happened on the server.
- Impact accuracy is perfect on this benchmark, so it shows no room to improve yet. The repair stages are where failures are expected.
- Only direct dependencies are checked for breaking changes; advisories cover the whole installed tree.

content.text:
Here's your interview prep. Every number below comes from your build log, so you can say all of it with confidence.

## First: the demo

The live site is still down, so don't plan to demo `veritas.milliebanned.xyz`. Pick one of these as a backup before you go on:
- **Run it on your Mac:** `npm run serve`, then open http://localhost:3210 and investigate one of your own benchmark repos. The express case takes about 40 seconds. Local mode is safe here because you wrote those repos.
- **Screenshots:** `evidence/ui/` has the app, and `evidence/neatlogs/` has the incident and pull request #2 opened by `neatlogs[bot]`.

Do one run before the interview so nothing surprises you live.

## The 30-second pitch

> "Veritas is an agent that tells you whether a dependency upgrade actually breaks *your* repo, and proves it. It reads the release notes and advisories, finds where you use the package, runs your tests before and after the upgrade, writes a fix, and only calls it fixed when your own tests pass again. The model proposes, the tests decide."

## The stories to tell

**1. neatlogs found a bug I couldn't see.**
> "The benchmark said everything passed. But neatlogs flagged one run: 12 of my agent's 14 edits were being refused. The run still ended green, so I'd never have noticed. neat AI investigated it and opened the fix as a pull request itself. Refused edits went from 12 to 0, cost from 14 cents to 5."

Only tell the next part if they ask for depth: neat AI's first theory was wrong. You showed it the evidence (every refused edit was off by exactly two spaces of indentation) and it revised the fix. That shows you checked the tool instead of trusting it blindly.

**2. A real failure that became a fix.**
> "My hardest test case, node-fetch 2 to 3, failed. Three attempts, then the agent said 'unresolved' instead of pretending. The cause: the upgrade guide that says the timeout option was removed was never fetched. neatlogs flagged it, neat AI opened PR #5, and after that it went from never fixed to fixed on the first try, at less than half the cost."

**3. cfo.ai said my pricing lost money.**
> "My first free plan gave five investigations a day on the expensive model. cfo.ai showed I lost money on every customer. I capped the free plan and moved it to the small model, and now it's profitable from month one with over 12 months of runway."

## The numbers to remember

- **9 of 9** verdicts correct
- **7 of 7** breaking upgrades fixed, all on the first attempt, each checked by a test the agent never sees
- **0** false positives on the control repos
- **$0.80** and about 4 minutes for the whole benchmark

## "Strategy and tips for winning"

They said they'd ask this, so have 2–3 ready:
- **"Use the sponsor tools for real, not for show."** You made a rule early: if neatlogs, Entire or cfo.ai can genuinely do something, use them for it. Two of your biggest improvements came straight out of neatlogs.
- **"Measure before and after."** Every fix has a before/after table. Judges can see what changed instead of taking your word for it.
- **"Be honest about what doesn't work."** The README lists what isn't built and where it's weak. You think that helped, because judges could trust the rest.
- **"Build a benchmark with known answers on day one."** Nine small repos with held-out tests meant every change could be checked in minutes.
- **"Keep a build log as you go."** It made the submission easy and gave judges the full story.

## Questions they might ask

**"Why did you build this?"**
Dependabot and similar tools tell you *something* changed. Nobody tells you whether it breaks *your* code. Veritas answers that with proof. If you have a personal story about a broken upgrade, use it here, because it lands better than anything I can write.

**"What was hardest?"**
Case 9. The agent needed facts that weren't in the release notes, and its diagnoses kept going in circles. That taught you the model is only as good as the sources it gets.

**"Why not just let the model decide if it's fixed?"**
> "Because models are confidently wrong. The tests are the only thing I trust. A fix only counts if tests that failed after the upgrade pass again."

**"What's weak?"**
Say it plainly; it'll come across well.
- Precision on affected files: 13 of 17 flagged files really needed changing. It sometimes flags test files that don't.
- No repair has yet failed and then recovered on a real run.
- It only supports npm, with no monorepos.

**"What's next?"**
> "Running it on real public repos like winston and yargs, opening the pull requests automatically, and signing three design partners before building anything else to sell."

**"How did you use Entire?"**
The agent uses `entire graph` while it runs to find where each package is used and to judge test runs. Every commit carries a checkpoint, viewable publicly at entire.io/gh/Milliebanned/Veritas.

**"Solo?"**
Yes, the build log says solo. Own it: one person, one weekend, nine states, 84 tests.

## Delivery tips

- Lead with the neatlogs story. It's their event, and that's the best example of their product working.
- Keep each answer under a minute, then stop. They can ask follow-ups.
- Don't read from notes. Know the four numbers and the three stories, and talk from there.

Good luck. You've got a great story to tell.

If they ask about the tools, give each one a short answer: what you used it for, a moment where it helped, and one honest piece of feedback. Sponsors love hearing all three.

## neatlogs (their event, so give this one the most time)

**What you used it for:**
> "Every run of Veritas is traced in neatlogs: each model call, each tool call, each state of the agent, with tokens, cost and time. The agent's prompts are neatlogs managed prompts, so I could version them without redeploying. And I set up detections, rules that flag a bad run automatically."

**The moment it helped:**
> "The best moment of the whole hackathon was neatlogs catching a bug I didn't know I had. My benchmark said everything passed. But a detection flagged one run where 12 of 14 edits were refused. neat AI read the trace, read my code, and opened a pull request with the fix. Refused edits went to zero and that case got almost three times cheaper. Later it did it again on my hardest case, which went from never fixed to fixed first try."

**What you liked:**
> "It closes the loop. Normally observability tells you something went wrong and you're on your own. Here it went from trace, to diagnosis, to an actual pull request."

**Honest feedback, if they ask what could be better.** Pick one or two:
- "neat AI's first diagnosis was wrong. Once I gave it the evidence from the trace, it got it right. So it works best as a partner, not on autopilot."
- "On day one, traces got stuck in 'processing' for a few hours, so I kept a local copy of every span as a backup."
- "Cost showed as $0 on my traces even though token counts were right."
- "The neat AI chat hit its length limit when the fix touched bigger files. It worked once I kept the change to one small file."

## Entire

**What you used it for:**
> "Two ways. First, inside the agent: Veritas uses entire-graph to find exactly where a package is used in a repo, who calls those functions, and which functions a fix touched. Second, for the build itself: every commit has a checkpoint linking it to the session that wrote it, and anyone can browse them publicly on entire.io."

**The moment it helped:**
> "The graph is how the agent knows which files to look at. On the express upgrade it found all four call sites with the right line numbers, and it correctly ignored a decoy file that looked related but wasn't."

**Honest feedback:**
- "`graph verify` reads Jest-style output, so with Node's built-in test runner it couldn't catch a regression. I kept the project's own tests as the source of truth."
- "Getting the repo mirrored needed my Entire account linked to GitHub. I'd signed up with Google, so that took a moment to figure out."
- "Honestly, I used the graph more inside my agent than while building it. It's a habit you have to build."

## cfo.ai

**What you used it for:**
> "I built the whole business plan in cfo.ai: pricing, model cost per investigation, revenue and runway. I used my real measured cost per run, not made-up numbers."

**The moment it helped:**
> "It showed me my first pricing lost money on every customer, because the free plan was too generous on an expensive model. I capped it and moved it to the small model, and the revised plan is profitable from month one, with over a year of runway."

**Honest feedback:**
> "Nobody has paid yet, so the prices are still hypotheses. But having the model meant I could change one number and see the whole plan move."

## If they ask about all three in one breath

> "neatlogs showed me what my agent was really doing and fixed two bugs with me. Entire gave my agent a map of the code. And cfo.ai told me my business model was broken before a customer did. Each one changed the project, not just decorated it."

Lead with the neatlogs story. It's their stage, and it's your strongest one.

You have access to browser automation tools (mcp__claude-in-chrome__*) for interacting with web pages in Chrome. Follow these guidelines for effective browser automation.

## Loading deferred tools

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback
* Name the file meaningfully to help the user identify it later (e.g., "login_process.gif")

## Console log debugging

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:

- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration

- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

The official Render docs and most secondary sources agree on the core free-tier limits, though some third-party pages contain stale or conflicting details.

- **RAM and CPU:** Free web services get 512 MB of RAM and 0.1 CPU. Free: 512 MB RAM, 0.1 CPU, per Render's compute plans page.
- **Spin-down:** Render's own docs say the service sleeps after 15 minutes with no inbound traffic, including HTTP requests and WebSocket messages (Render spins down a Free web service that goes 15 minutes without receiving any inbound traffic. This includes both HTTP requests and WebSocket messages from existing connections.). Waking it takes about a minute. One aggregator says the window was 30 minutes before a 2025 change, but I could not confirm that against Render's changelog.
- **Hours:** Each workspace gets 750 free instance hours a month across its Free web services, according to a pricing review.
- **Filesystem:** The free tier's filesystem is ephemeral. Local files, such as uploads or SQLite databases, are wiped on redeploy, restart, or spin-down (per Render's free docs).
- **Persistent disk:** Free web services cannot attach a persistent disk. Paid services can (Paid services can also preserve local filesystem changes by attaching a persistent disk, but Free web services cannot.). For file storage, Render's FAQ recommends a persistent disk, and for relational data it recommends Render Postgres.
- **Paid upgrade:** A paid instance avoids the spin-down. Third-party sources put the cheapest paid web instance at $7/month, but their RAM and price figures disagree with each other, so check Render's pricing page before relying on them.

content.text:
Render works for the website, but not for running the agent on public repos. Render's free plan gives you:

- **512 MB of RAM and a tenth of a CPU.** That's very little. Your own small benchmark repos would probably still run, slowly. Real repos like winston would likely run out of memory during `npm install`.
- **No Docker inside your app.** Veritas would have to run repos' test code in the same container that holds your model API key, with nothing in between. For public repos you didn't write, that means one bad repo could steal the key. I wouldn't do it.
- **History that gets wiped.** The database lives in a SQLite file, and Render deletes local files whenever the app restarts, redeploys or goes to sleep. So past investigations would vanish.
- **Sleep after 15 minutes without visitors.** The next visitor waits about a minute for it to wake up.

The landing page, the benchmark numbers and the design would all work fine, so for a portfolio link it's OK.

**What I'd do instead:**

1. **For the site:** put it on Render in a "showcase" setup, with the landing page plus runs on your own benchmark repos only, no pasting public GitHub URLs. Signup is just "sign in with GitHub", which is easy. I'd add a Dockerfile and a `render.yaml` to the repo, and you'd click "New → Blueprint" and point it at the repo. Then you point `veritas.milliebanned.xyz` at Render.
2. **For testing on public repos:** that needs a real machine with Docker. The easiest free one is your Mac with **Docker Desktop** installed. Then I can run winston, luxon, yargs and the others here safely in containers. No cloud account needed.

**Want me to set up the Render version?** I'd add the Dockerfile and config on a new branch and limit investigations to your benchmark repos. You'd click deploy.

Sources:
- [Render: Deploy for Free](https://render.com/docs/free)
- [Render: compute plans](https://render.com/docs/compute-plans.md)
- [Render FAQ](https://render.com/docs/faq)
- [temps.sh: Render pricing 2026](https://temps.sh/blog/render-pricing-2026)

**For running the agent on public repos:**

**GitHub Codespaces** (recommended)

content.text: what do you mean show case only?

"Showcase only" means the site would be up and look complete, but visitors couldn't use it on their own repos.

**What would work:**
- The landing page: what Veritas does, the benchmark numbers, how neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai are used.
- The full app: starting an investigation and watching it go through each step, findings, the patch review with before and after test runs, and the report.
- Running it on **your own benchmark repos** (express, chalk, node-fetch and the rest). You wrote those, so it's safe to run their code.

**What would be switched off:**
- Pasting **someone else's GitHub repo** and running Veritas on it.

**Why:** Veritas installs a repo and runs that repo's tests. Running tests means running whatever code is in the repo, and you don't know what's in a stranger's repo.

- On a real server with Docker, that code runs inside a locked container. It has no network, can't see your API keys, and can't touch anything else.
- On Render or Hugging Face there's no Docker. The repo's code would run right next to Veritas, which holds your model API key, so a bad repo could steal the key and run up your bill.

So on those free hosts, I'd limit the site to your benchmark repos.

Here's a practical comparison:
- **Showcase (Render or Hugging Face, free):** good for a portfolio link, or for someone to click around and see a real run.
- **Full version (Codespaces, Hetzner or AWS):** needed if you want people, or me, to run it on real public repos like winston or yargs.
